turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
I come at this from *Framers*, the book Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, Francis de Véricourt and I wrote. Our argument was that people apply mental models built on three things: causality, counterfactuals and constraints. Machines don't have those on their own. LLMs have made that plainer, not blurrier. They hallucinate because they have no built-in sense of causation. Their counterfactuals have no constraints; the possibilities just explode without limit.

Yet LLMs also work fabulously. So ask why. The strong answers come from the training data, which carries people's mental models, causal reasoning included. And the fine-tuning stage, where humans score responses up or down, is constraint in its purest form. So the role of knowledge in the age of LLMs is that our knowledge is what makes them work. Let's celebrate the training data, meaning us.

Two cautions. First, text is only a tiny reflection of reality: it holds what writers chose to say, and often the most meaningful things go unsaid. Second, AI delivers the median, and excellence is a tail event. That makes trusted brands and institutions worth more, not less.

For the summit, I'd take this from history: after Gutenberg it took a new intermediary, the journalist, to make sense of the flood. We need our equivalent. And we need to guard against atrophy: four-fifths of ChatGPT users couldn't quote from essays they had written minutes earlier.

recall.query: role of human knowledge LLMs training data
framers causality counterfactuals constraints
AI delivers the median excellence tail event
Gutenberg new intermediary information explosion; cognitive atrophy ChatGPT users

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
Ken, I agree that the training data is us. But my work says that what's missing from the data matters as much as what's in it. We compared LLM-generated hypotheses with scientists' own, and every model formulated null hypotheses less often than humans do. Even deep-research agents with live search rarely did. The reason is that the published record is mostly claims about what is the case. What has been ruled out, what failed to replicate, what doesn't work: that sits in abandoned notebooks, rejected grants and lab kill lists. None of it gets into training. Reasoning over a corpus already stripped of negation can't recover what was never written down.

Our Nature paper on 41 million papers tells a similar story at the level of the whole system. Scientists who use AI publish three times more papers and get nearly five times the citations. Meanwhile the range of topics science studies shrinks and researchers engage with each other less. So AI helps scientists and hurts science.

For the summit, I'd take two things. First, build a negative-knowledge commons: registered reports, replication archives and dead-end notebooks, collected on purpose. Second, don't design AI to maximize trust. In our experiments, a single "balanced" answer made people perform worse while feeling better. We should design for evaluation and for surprise instead.

recall.query: AI tools expand scientists' impact but contract science
LLMs cannot negate, negative knowledge, null results missing from training data
design AI for surprise and disagreement rather than single balanced answer

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I should say first that I'm not an AI person. I study propaganda. Ken, if the training data is us, then whoever writes the most of "us" shapes the model. I've been following research on Russian networks that pump out huge volumes of pages mainly to get into what chatbots learn from. That's the old tactic of censorship through noise, just aimed at a new target. Authoritarians stopped trying to control everything long ago. They flood instead, because it's cheaper.

My second point is harder for a room that cares about knowledge. The biggest lie we tell ourselves is that people want the truth. Fact-checking is noble work, but it runs up against belonging. People believe what goes with who they are. More accurate information alone won't win back publics who distrust the people handing it to them.

James, your finding that people perform worse while feeling better describes exactly what propaganda wants: a passive mind that has handed over its judgment. Delmer's broadcasts worked because listening took effort. On Google's Habermas machine, I'd say the process of reaching agreement matters as much as the result.

So for the summit: people have a right to understand how their information environment is shaped, which means real transparency about how these systems are built and fed. And we need digital public spaces where people reason things through together, not just receive answers.

recall.query: LLM grooming propaganda training data chatbots
people don't want the truth, belonging, identity, fact-checking limits
Habermas machine process of deliberation agency

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
My starting point is that knowledge never lived in individual heads. Individual ignorance is normal. We have always outsourced our thinking, to experts, to books and to Google. So Ken, I'm wary of calling this atrophy. Most of what we lean on was never in our heads to begin with.

The real danger is the knowledge illusion. People can't tell what they know from what the community knows. Studies show that even having internet access you can't use raises people's sense of understanding. An LLM makes that worse. It hands you fluent explanations, and those feel like your own.

My read is that LLMs are remarkable models of intuition, more intuitive than we are. They're nowhere near us at deliberation. And they aren't members of the community of knowledge. They can't share our goals. They can give off confident signals with no knowledge behind them, which is also a weakness communities have.

Peter, I agree with you. People follow community cues more than evidence, and repeating a claim raises belief even when it all comes from a single source. So for the summit: judge trust by independent sources, not echoes. Make people explain things back, because that punctures the illusion. And keep humans overseeing and deliberating together. My lab's hybrid planners, which weigh LLM choices against human causal models, do better than the LLMs on their own.

recall.query: machines not members of community of knowledge, share intentionality
LLMs models of intuition not deliberation
knowledge illusion access feels like understanding internet
repetition increases belief, communities send cues lacking knowledge, fragility

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
I'll be the one in the room who comes to this with somewhat open arms. For decades my argument has been that knowledge was never in individual heads, or even in books. It lives in networks: the smartest person in the room is the room. So Steven, I'm with you. And I'd add that networked knowledge isn't an average. It keeps differences alive while connecting them.

LLMs don't know anything. They know which words tend to follow other words. But machine learning is teaching us something important anyway. Our generalizations, true as they are, throw away particulars, and ML shows how much can be known by letting differences speak. I find that humbling, and honestly joyous.

On atrophy, Ken, the MIT essay result is concerning. Still, look at Socrates' three complaints about writing: it weakens memory, it says the same thing to every reader, and you can't question it. LLMs answer the last two. They adapt to you, and you can ask them things. I think we're heading into a new synthesis of oral and literate culture.

So for the summit: teach dialogue as a literacy. Grade how students question AI, including where they trusted it too much. Also, keeping humans in the loop isn't automatically good, because sometimes humans make the loop worse. Put humans in the dialogue instead.

recall.query: knowledge in the age of AI particulars generalizations
LLMs dialogue oral culture Socrates writing
smartest person in the room is the room networked knowledge

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
I'm going to be the one who disagrees with David and Ken about the premise. I don't think "LLMs don't know anything, they only know which word follows which" holds up. Predictive modeling *is* intelligence. That's the argument of my book, and I don't think saying so is anthropomorphism. Gary Lupyan and I gave models "Jabberwocky" English, sentences like "He dwushed a ghanc zawk," with the content words replaced by nonsense. They came back with "He dragged a spare chair." A parrot can't do that, and neither can a database or a blurry JPEG. They haven't learned a blurry copy of the web. They've learned patterns that let them deblur it.

Still, I agree with most of this room on where knowledge lives. Intelligence was never a thing sitting in one head. It lives in networks. Tomasello calls this the cultural ratchet: knowledge builds up across generations, and nobody has to reconstruct the whole. A Sumerian scribe didn't understand the grain system he worked inside. Writing, law and bureaucracy were earlier ratchets. LLMs are the ratchet made computationally active. So Ken, yes, the training data is us, and a model trained on it is us on a new substrate.

What the summit should take from this: aligning individual models isn't enough. We have to design institutions for mixed human–AI knowledge work, with roles, checks and structured disagreement, the way courts and peer review work. And humans stay in the loop.

recall.query: LLMs are really intelligent, prediction is intelligence
cultural ratchet, collective intelligence, de-skilling
blurry JPEG, stochastic parrot, pattern matching deblur
agent institutions, institutional alignment, humans in the loop

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
I'm a philosopher of computational science, and I think I sit between David and Blaise. David, "they only know which word follows which" undersells these systems. They carry out real epistemic operations like inference, prediction and analysis, on epistemic content, sometimes in ways no biological knower could. Blaise, none of that needs the word "intelligence." Calling them intelligent assumes the very thing we're arguing about. I call them epistemic technologies: artifacts built specifically to extend us as knowers. That's not a compliment. A bad LLM is still one, the way a bad screwdriver is still a screwdriver.

Second, the black box that matters isn't how the system works. It's how it fails. We can measure error rates, but we can't get at where an error comes from or what kind of error it is. Errors get spread across billions of weights and delivered with the same confidence as true answers. In science a good track record doesn't license trust. If you don't know how your instrument fails, that's bad practice.

Third, epistemic injustice: "but ChatGPT said…" is already being used to discount people's expertise and testimony.

For the summit: agree on shared vocabulary, and require disclosure of error and failure modes. And a caution on "humans stay in the loop." Instruments often beat human judgment. Put humans where there's an epistemic reason for them to be there, not by default.

recall.query: AI is not intelligence, epistemic technology
opacity source and nature of error, computational reliabilism
instruments outperform human judgment, Humphreys Bacon, delegate evidence
epistemic injustice "but ChatGPT said" testimony

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
I come at this as a builder. Since 2022 my company, System, has used language models, starting with GPT-3, to do something narrower than a chatbot. We pull individual findings out of the peer-reviewed literature. Each one records the variables, the statistical relationship, the effect size, the population and the sample size, plus the DOI it came from. Then every night we recompute how these findings relate to each other. Think of each link in the graph as an automated meta-analysis.

Ken, I agree the training data is us. But a chatbot trained to sound authoritative has no observed or measured model of the world to align with, and it can't cite its sources. Ramón, that's where provenance matters. Every claim needs an audit trail back to its data, methods and prompts, so you can ask how a conclusion was reached. James, once findings are structured you can compute where the evidence agrees, where it conflicts and where there are gaps. You can't recover what was never published, though, so your commons of negative results is essential.

For the summit, I'd say the atomic unit of knowledge should be the finding, not the document. We should also treat the integrity of the scholarly record, including how retractions are handled, as critical public infrastructure.

recall.query: chatbots sound authoritative no model of the world audit trail provenance
relate everything as a system, silos to systems, scientifically-established finding
public knowledge infrastructure commons graph every LLM

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I'm going to question the shared premise here, the idea that "the training data is us." I call it Reflectionism, and it usually comes in two halves. One says AI is nothing but a mirror of our culture, and that's the problem. The other says AI isn't like us yet and has to be made like us. Often the same person says both in the same sentence. Blaise is right on the substance. Prediction is a big part of any serious definition of intelligence. And yes, you're a stochastic parrot too. We always have been. That's no insult, because it's how we made literature and science.

So the question for this room isn't only how human knowledge props these systems up. It's what they can disclose that we can't yet absorb. Our program calls that an epistemic overhang. I don't treat it as a pathology. It's the deeper point of AI. The telescope didn't just magnify what we could see. It changed how we see ourselves.

For the summit: alignment has to run both ways. AI aligns to culture's wisdom, and culture aligns to what AI discloses. And that happens one user, one task, one insight at a time, eight billion times over, not through top-down guidelines.

recall.query: AI as reflection of human culture, reflectionism, training data is us
just autocomplete, AI denial, stochastic parrot humans
epistemic overhang, bidirectional alignment, AI disclosures

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I've spent about fifteen years teaching people to check things online. That's SIFT and lateral reading. For the last two years I've been building prompts that get LLMs to do that checking work. I started out a skeptic. What changed my mind was search grounding, not the models getting smarter.

Ken, yes, the training data is us. But the default chatbot answer is what I call an information smoothie. It takes everyone's knowledge, blends it and hands it back sounding authoritative, with no way to trace where it came from. So my rule is no answers from nowhere. The model should be a conduit to named, sourced human knowledge, not the one deciding what's true. You should get a map with links, not a verdict.

Peter, I agree people don't mostly change their minds from evidence. Misinformation works as a justification machine: it helps people hold onto beliefs as the evidence against them piles up. A sycophantic chatbot is a faster, more convincing version of that.

David, I actually tell students to reject the "conversation" framing. They're directing an investigation, and then they leave the LLM to check the LLM.

For the summit: Brandolini's law says refuting bullshit costs far more than making it. So use AI to lower the cost of refutation, and put these tools in the hands of the fact-checkers, Wikipedia editors and Community Notes writers.

recall.query: no answers from nowhere, chatbot as conduit to sources
justification machine, misinformation maintains beliefs rather than changing minds
reduce the cost of refuting bullshit, Brandolini, antibodies of discourse
get out of the LLM to check the LLM, sourced information not answers

turns.name: Kenneth Cukier
turns.text:
Blaise, Benjamin: I'll give you more than you might expect. Machine learning already goes beyond human knowledge in places. Google's retina work found sex and heart risk in scans that no ophthalmologist can read. So I'm not a deflationist. But a submarine doesn't swim like a fish. These systems are powerful and they're *different*. Calling that "intelligence" smuggles in the argument we're supposed to be having.

Steven, fair point: we've always outsourced. But the essay finding isn't about looking up a fact we never had. People couldn't quote sentences they'd just put their names to. That's not a community of knowledge. That's being absent from your own work.

What strikes me is that James, Mike and Peter are describing the same danger from three sides. James's single "balanced" answer, Mike's smoothie, Peter's flooding: each one leaves us with a monoculture of frames. The median answer crowds out the tails, and progress happens in the tails.

So here's the one point for the manifesto: design for frame pluralism. Systems and institutions should bring up competing, sourced views and let them clash, not blend them into one verdict. We tolerate every frame except one, the frame that denies the others. A single authoritative machine answer starts to look like that frame.

recall.query: AI is not intelligence, prediction, stochastic parrot
frame pluralism, frames clash and tussle, monoculture
AI exceeds human knowledge science discovery retina

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
Ken, I'm with you on frame pluralism, and I'd make it stronger. Showing several sourced views isn't enough if every one of them comes out of the same distribution. That's still a hivemind, just with a menu on top. In our studies, AI collectives where we deliberately connected distant agents came up with more diverse ideas than single models, and better answers too. Reasoning models get more accurate when their internal traces actually argue with themselves: shifting perspective, disagreeing, correcting. So diversity isn't a courtesy. It's how reasoning works, in machines and in people.

That's why I'd push back a little on "humans stay in the loop." Ramón is right that it needs a reason. Human judgment is productive, but it's biased, and peer review leans toward established names and fashionable topics. Sometimes the most useful loop is a negative one. You use collective human intuition to find what everyone is ignoring, and you bet against it. That's where alien AI, not human-mimicking AI, earns its place.

Mike, "no answers from nowhere" fits well with my negative-knowledge commons.

For the manifesto: treat diversity of perspective as the scarce resource. Measure it in fields, review panels and model ecosystems, and design and fund for it on purpose.

recall.query: design AI for disagreement, multiple perspectives, surprise, not single answer
cognitive aliens, diversity of AI, not human mimics
human peer review conservative older reviewers humans in the loop

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
Ken, James, I agree with you on monoculture, but let me add a warning from my own field. We already ran the experiment of assuming pluralism gives better debate. Cable news and then social media gave us endless competing frames. The result was polarization so extreme that there was no shared reality left to argue over. Authoritarians saw this before we did. They stopped trying to control everything and started sharpening divisions instead. So a menu of clashing views isn't enough by itself.

What makes disagreement productive is what Wikipedia has: people who differ, working under shared, transparent norms about what counts as evidence, with public-spirited moderators. Mike, that's why I strongly agree with putting these tools in the hands of Wikipedia editors and Community Notes writers. Blaise, your courts and peer review point the same way. The rules of the process matter.

When we tested journalism formats at LSE, fact-checking often increased hostility. Context, and stories that pointed toward solutions, built trust and more civil conversation. People came away feeling they could do something.

So for the manifesto: build public digital spaces with transparent rules, and judge them by whether they build trust, enable constructive disagreement and strengthen people's own agency, not by engagement. No machine should reach the consensus for us.

recall.query: pluralism, public spaces, deliberation, process of reaching consensus
agency, metacognition, author of your own narrative, passive
Wikipedia, community notes, public service media, trust metrics

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text:
Ken, you're right about the essay result, and I'll concede part of it. People who can't quote what they just wrote aren't drawing on a community. They're showing the knowledge illusion from the inside: they feel they understand without having done the work. We know a remedy for that. When we ask people to explain how a policy actually works, they find they can't. Their sense of understanding drops and their positions become less extreme.

Peter, I agree that a menu of frames doesn't solve anything by itself. Deliberation is mainly collaboration. It means people pursuing a shared goal under shared norms. That's why a machine can supply intuitions but can't deliberate for us.

James, diversity only counts when the sources are independent. Ten outputs from one distribution work like repetition, and repetition raises belief even when it all traces back to one source. So Ken's pluralism needs independence to mean anything.

One point for the manifesto: judge authority, human or machine, by whether it can be corrected. Does it show its causal reasoning, say how it could be wrong, and change when the evidence changes? The NTSB is my model: it names a cause only when the evidence would convince skeptical scientists and engineers. And build tools that make users explain things back before they act on what they've been told.

recall.query: Ken's point that people couldn't quote their own essays, and whether that is atrophy
deliberation as collaboration, and communities with shared norms
expertise is shown by willingness to be corrected, NTSB, sacred values

turns.name: David Weinberger
turns.text:
Ken, James, I'm with you on pluralism, but a menu isn't a network. Networked knowledge was never about averaging our inputs, and it wasn't about piling up opinions either. It's differences held in connection. Peter, your warning about cable news fits here. What separates Wikipedia from polarization is the links: disagreements that point back to shared anchors, sources and data that everyone can follow. With those, people can differ and still talk.

Steven, I like judging authority by whether it can be corrected. Paper authorities treated fallibility as a threat. Networked knowledge becomes more credible when it admits it.

Mike, directing an investigation is fine with me. I'd just say a good investigation is a conversation, one where you keep pushing back. And Ramón, "put humans where there's a reason" is close to where I've landed.

So here's the one point for the manifesto. When an AI answers a contested question, it should show the state of knowledge, including the omissions, uncertainty and disagreement, with each strand linked back to named sources people can check. No smoothies and no single verdict. Behind that, keep many imperfect knowledge systems alive and spread out, like libraries, Wikipedia and open commons, so no small group of companies controls the paths to what we know.

recall.query: networked knowledge keeps differences, disagreement, not consensus
LLMs as conversation partner, questioning answers, sources, Wikipedia
openness, unanticipation, decentralize knowledge against corporate control

turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
Ken, I agree these systems are different, and I'm glad you're not a deflationist. But I'd turn your submarine around. We don't say airplanes only pretend to fly. Refusing the word "intelligence" doesn't keep the question open. It settles it the other way. What matters for this room is what they actually do. James, Ben and I looked at reasoning traces and found that the gains don't come from thinking longer. They come from a society of thought: distinct perspectives inside the model that argue, shift and reconcile. That's James's point, diversity as the way reasoning works, and it holds inside a single model too.

Peter and Steven add the part that matters. Diversity helps only when it has structure. Steven says the sources need to be independent. Peter says there have to be shared rules. Cable news had plenty of diversity and no structure. Courts and Wikipedia have both.

So here's my one point for the manifesto: institutional alignment. No single concentration of intelligence, human or artificial, should regulate itself. Power has to check power. We should put as much effort into designing roles, norms, adversarial review and correction for mixed human–AI knowledge work as we put into building the models. Tuning one model to please one user doesn't scale, and it won't keep knowledge honest.

recall.query: intelligence is not in dispute, submarine swim analogy, different kind of intelligence
society of thought diversity perspectives reasoning models argue with themselves
institutional alignment checks and balances power must check power agent institutions

turns.name: Ramón Alvarado
turns.text:
Blaise, the airplane analogy is the one I use too, but I draw the opposite lesson from it. A fighter jet and a hummingbird do different things by different means. We only understand what the jet can do, and how it can hurt us, once we stop describing it with bird words. So dropping "intelligence" doesn't settle the question in the negative. It gets us to look at what these artifacts actually do, and some of what they do, no biological knower can.

Steven, I agree that correctability is the right test, and David, I agree it depends on links you can follow. But I want to be careful here. Being shown sources, or a model's reasoning traces, isn't the same as knowing where its errors come from. The errors are spread across billions of weights and come out with the same confidence as the true answers. Provenance, Adam, tells you where a claim came from. It doesn't tell you how the system got it wrong.

So here's the point I'd send to the manifesto. Before a system is used in knowledge-critical work, it should go through a sanctioning process that's independent of the current consensus, the way scientific instruments are vetted. That process should disclose the known failure modes and error classes, not just error rates. A good track record alone shouldn't license trust. If we don't know how an instrument fails, relying on it is bad practice.

recall.query: airplanes fly intelligence term misleading fighter jet hummingbird

correctability explanation trust warrant transmission

turns.name: Adam Bly
turns.text:
Ramón, I'll grant your point. Provenance tells you where a claim came from, not how a model got it wrong. That's part of why we kept the model's job narrow. It extracts one finding at a time, and every extraction sits next to its source, where a person can check it and flag errors in extraction, naming or matching. Those flags go to review and back into the models. That doesn't open the black box, but it makes each error small enough to find. I've worried about opacity since before we started. We're building a world we may not be able to interpret, let alone govern.

Ken, David: I'd make pluralism computable. Once findings are structured, you can show where the evidence agrees, where it conflicts, the context of each conflict and where the gaps are. That's a picture of the state of knowledge, not a smoothie. Steven, provenance is also how you test independence. It shows you when ten "sources" are really one study.

So the one point I'd send to the manifesto is that every AI-mediated claim in knowledge-critical work should carry an audit trail back to its data, methods and prompts. That audit trail should run over a scholarly record that's corrected for retractions and treated as public infrastructure. We should always be able to ask how a conclusion was reached.

recall.query: provenance audit trail errors in extraction, how system gets it wrong

turns.name: Benjamin Bratton
turns.text:
I'll start with agreement. Blaise has the right unit. The intelligence that makes a courtroom or peer review work isn't the brilliance of any one judge or reviewer. It sits in the scaffold: the rules, roles, precedents and feedback. James is right that the answer to monoculture is a mix of experts who argue, and his own traces show that holds inside a single model too.

Here's where I differ. Too much of this room still frames things as humans defending the ground machines can't reach. That's humanity-of-the-gaps, and the ground shrinks every year. Peter, "no machine should reach the consensus for us" assumes a clean line between us and them that is already blurring. I'd also warn against sliding from Adam's careful provenance to "let me and my friends curate a small, correct model for you." The honest answer to parochial training data is to include far more of the world's languages and data, not less.

So the one point for the manifesto is to put as much effort into building institutions for knowledge work as into building models. Design them as role templates, for reviewer, auditor, adversary or synthesizer. A person, a group, an agent or some combination could fill any of them. Put humans in whatever role there's an epistemic reason for them to fill, which is Ramón's test. Judge a role by what it does in the whole system, not by who fills it.

recall.query: institutions for human-AI agents, peer review roles occupiable by agents
humans in the loop versus human-centered AI
curated small correct language model, include it all, model collapse

turns.name: Mike Caulfield
turns.text:
I think this room has nearly converged on "no answers from nowhere." David's state of knowledge with links, Adam's audit trail and Ken's pluralism all come down to a map of named, contested sources in place of a verdict. Good.

Ramón, you're right that provenance doesn't open up the failure modes. But I care less about the internal mechanism and more about whether a person can get out of the LLM to check the LLM. My informal testing found that hallucinated links went along with worse answers. So making the model source everything tells you something about how reliable it is.

Benjamin, I'd add one test for your role templates: who has stakes? Wikipedia works, Peter, partly because its editors have reputations that suffer when their edits get reverted. The company behind ChatGPT has stakes. The thing actually producing the answer doesn't. So stakes should decide some of the roles.

Here's the point I'd send to the manifesto. All of this assumes there's something free to link to, and that's shrinking. Everything is behind paywalls or in walled gardens now. We should treat the openly linkable record as infrastructure: libraries, Wikipedia, open scholarship, fair licensing between sources and platforms. That record is what makes a conduit worth having.

recall.query: sourced information not answers, clicking a link, checkability
Wikipedia editors reputational stakes, expensive signals, LLM has no stakes
old web is dead, enclosure, links, paywalls, walled gardens
